# Pretraining a small time-series foundation model from scratch: a research note

*Generated by `tsfm docs build` from committed results. Every number below is read from
a file under `results/`.*

## Question

Can a small decoder-only transformer, pretrained from scratch only on public data that
we have checked for overlap with the benchmark, forecast unseen series zero-shot better
than classical per-series baselines on GIFT-Eval? How does accuracy change with model
size and compute, and with the choice of tokenizer?

## Data

See `DATA_CARD.md`. Two findings matter for anyone using the same corpus:

1. The upstream pretraining collection, described as non-leaking, contains exact or
   rescaled copies of GIFT-Eval series (Australian weather vs `temperature_rain`, Beijing
   air quality vs `kdd_cup_2018`, several Monash monthly sets and FRED-MD vs `m4_monthly`,
   pedestrian counts vs `m4_hourly`), some inside GIFT-Eval's test windows. We excluded
   every flagged series; numbers are in the data card.
2. A naive window-hash check also produces false matches from linearly interpolated
   gaps, which look identical in every series after normalisation; these must be
   filtered or inspected, not counted as leakage.

## Method

Decoder-only transformer, pre-norm RMSNorm, rotary positions, SwiGLU, KV cache, in plain
PyTorch. Two tokenizers: (a) mean scaling and 4,096-token quantisation with
cross-entropy, sampled autoregressively; (b) patches with a non-crossing quantile head,
rolled out by feeding back medians. Training samples a random context length per window
and computes the scale from the context only. Evaluation follows GIFT-Eval exactly (our
Seasonal Naive reproduces upstream's on all official metrics and configurations).

### Fine-tuning on realized volatility, and regime robustness

Design fixed in `PREREGISTRATION_VOL.md` (tag `prereg-vol-v1`) before scoring: daily
realized volatility of BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT from Binance Vision 5-minute klines
(CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), 22-day forecasts from every day of the test period, pooled weighted
quantile loss with moving-block bootstrap intervals.

Our model was not run on this study before the deadline; the baselines were.

## Scope

`DEVIATIONS.md` records, before any T4 model was scored on the test split, what was
cut from that pre-registered plan: three model sizes instead of four to six, no
tokenizer conclusion, one seed, and no test-split scoring of `patch_s2`. The later CPU
study is a separate pre-registration. It did score its own model once.

## Not established

Things this project does **not** show, whatever the numbers above say:

* A test score for `patch_s2`. The test numbers in this note are the CPU model
  ({{ results/runs/cpu_s0_seed0/summary.json#params_total | int }} parameters). On that
  model, CRPS against Seasonal Naive is not distinguishable from 1, and both CRPS and
  MASE are worse than upstream AutoARIMA.
* That the CPU result would survive a larger training budget. It is {{ results/runs/cpu_s0_seed0/summary.json#config.train.steps | int }} steps on CPU.
* That the model is useful for any real forecasting or trading decision. Nothing here
  measures economic value, and no trading performance is claimed.
* That scaling trends continue beyond the sizes trained: the fit describes three runs.
* That the T4 headline holds across training seeds: `patch_s2` was scored with one seed.
  The CPU study has three seeds. Their test CRPS ratios are
  {{ results/analysis/cpu_study.json#test.crps_gmean_across_seeds.values.0 | .3f }},
  {{ results/analysis/cpu_study.json#test.crps_gmean_across_seeds.values.1 | .3f }} and
  {{ results/analysis/cpu_study.json#test.crps_gmean_across_seeds.values.2 | .3f }}.
  The mean of those three is
  {{ results/analysis/cpu_study.json#test.crps_gmean_across_seeds.mean | .3f }},
  and the Student-t interval on that mean is
  [{{ results/analysis/cpu_study.json#test.crps_gmean_across_seeds.ci95.0 | .3f }},
  {{ results/analysis/cpu_study.json#test.crps_gmean_across_seeds.ci95.1 | .3f }}].
  That is not the interval on the seed-averaged ratio.
* Which tokenizer is better: the comparison did not complete.
* That the corpus is free of *all* benchmark overlap: the check finds exact and affine
  copies, not noisy, warped or differently aggregated ones.
* That differences within a frequency, domain or horizon group are real: those
  breakdowns are descriptive and not corrected for multiple comparisons.
* That far-horizon intervals of the patch model are calibrated: median roll-outs ignore
  the uncertainty of earlier steps.
* Anything about users or adoption: there are none.
